title: Insist on yourself

segments.voice: Yesterday, trust thyself: the iron string, and our own rejected thoughts coming back in someone else's voice. Your line was trust thyself. Did you say one thought out loud before waving it off? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-five.

Music teachers meet this student now and then. They love one guitarist so much that they learn every lick, every bend, every bit of attitude. And they get good. Really good. Close your eyes and it almost sounds like the real thing. Almost. Then one day the teacher asks them to play something of their own, and the room goes quiet. They don't know what their own sounds like. They've spent years becoming a very good copy. Emerson has a sentence for that student, and it is short enough to write on the back of a hand: insist on yourself; never imitate.
screen: `A VERY GOOD COPY.` → `PLAY SOMETHING OF YOUR OWN.` → `INSIST ON YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: First, the line, from Self-Reliance: "Insist on yourself; never imitate." Two commands, one positive, one negative, and they are the same command seen from two sides. Second, his reason. Emerson says that your own gift you can offer at any moment with the force of a whole lifetime's cultivation behind it. But a talent borrowed from someone else, you only half own. You have to reach for it every time, and it's never quite there. The copy can be good. It just can't grow, because its roots are in someone else's life. Third, the great names. Emerson asks who could have taught Shakespeare to be Shakespeare. Nobody. And no amount of studying Shakespeare will make another one. In Emerson's telling, the great names he admires got there by doing what only they could do. So the way to honor someone you admire isn't to become them. It's to do with your life what they did with theirs. Fourth, a word about envy. Earlier in the same essay, Emerson writes that a person reaches a point where they're convinced that "envy is ignorance." Envy, he means, is not knowing your own portion. Wanting someone else's gift is a way of not looking at yours. None of this means don't learn from anyone. The guitar student should learn the licks. Emerson himself, in The American Scholar, called books the best of things, well used. The question is what happens next. Do the borrowed things become a ladder to your own voice, or a costume you never take off?
screen: `INSIST ON YOURSELF; NEVER IMITATE.` · `A BORROWED TALENT, HALF OWNED.` · `NOBODY COULD TEACH SHAKESPEARE.` · `ENVY IS IGNORANCE.` · then, large: `A LADDER, NOT A COSTUME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one thing to do your own way. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something ordinary you do every day. How you make coffee. How you write an email. How you greet people. How you pray, if you pray. Ask quietly: whose way is this? Did I choose it, or did I copy it from someone without noticing? There's no need to change anything yet. Just find one small place where your own way is waiting under a borrowed one. The bell holds the time.
Insist on yourself. Emerson's line from Self-Reliance: your own gift carries a lifetime behind it, and a borrowed one you only half own. Today's word.
Your line: never imitate. Today, take the one small thing you found and do it your own way, once, even if it comes out a little clumsy. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Some readers take 'insist on yourself; never imitate' as permission to learn from others while refusing to become a copy of them, letting what they borrow lead toward their own voice.

options: keep copying until you're as good as they are.
use what you learned to find what only you can do.

trapdoor: what you thought: never imitate means never learn from anyone.
what it means: learn from everyone, but let what you borrow lead to your own voice.
what a scholar hears: Emerson's argument rests on cultivation: your own gift has a lifetime behind it, while an adopted talent is an extemporaneous half possession.

notes: Confirm exact wording: 'Insist on yourself; never imitate.' and 'envy is ignorance' (from: 'there is a time in every man's education when he arrives at the conviction that envy is ignorance; that imitation is suicide...'). The script deliberately omits 'imitation is suicide' as a hard word for a wellness app; a reviewer may decide whether to include it.

Paraphrased: 'Your own gift you can present every moment with the cumulative force of a whole life's cultivation; but of the adopted talent of another you have only an extemporaneous half possession.' Confirm.
Emerson spells it 'Shakspeare'; the script uses the modern spelling in its own words.
'Emerson's own essays are full of the books he loved' is a general characterization; cut if a reviewer wants it sourced.
The guitar-student hook is an illustration, not a source claim.
